Why two investments do not make a simple average of risk: five views of diversification

Explore allocation curves, a risk–return scatter plot, a variance waterfall, signed risk contributions and a correlation matrix with editable two-asset assumptions.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore allocation weights, correlation and a two-asset risk picture

Interactive planning lab

Assumed one-year portfolio arithmetic mean5.60%
Calculated annual portfolio standard deviation8.67%
One standard deviation translated to the selected CAD amount$8,669.95

Original two-asset moment calculations, not historical data or forecasts. Weights are long-only and sum to 100%; no leverage, cash flows, fees, taxes, FX, trading restrictions or serial-return model is included. All return means, standard deviations and correlations are independently selected assumptions, without an estimated covariance matrix for any actual investment. Mean return is arithmetic over one year. Standard deviation measures dispersion; it is not a maximum loss, drawdown, loss probability or guaranteed range. Translating standard deviation to dollars changes the scale, not the investment risk percentage. Correlation stresses describe alternative assumptions and have no assigned probabilities. No distributional shape or normality is assumed.

The central idea

Portfolio return is a weighted arithmetic mean in this one-year model. Portfolio standard deviation also depends on how the two returns move together. Neither number establishes the right investment plan.

01

Define the returns before drawing the portfolio

Two portfolios with identical capital weights can have different risk when their investments behave differently together. This article isolates that relationship using two hypothetical assets, A and B. Neither name represents a fund, a security, a country or an asset-class forecast.

The example assigns 60% to A and 40% to B at the start of one year. A has an assumed arithmetic mean return of 4% and a return standard deviation of 6%. B has corresponding assumptions of 8% and 18%. Their assumed correlation is 0.2. These are chosen inputs for an explanation, rather than estimates extracted from market data.

The public CFA Institute portfolio-risk overview identifies individual risk, return and correlation as determinants of portfolio risk. The calculations below apply those general relationships to this independent example. They do not reproduce a historical portfolio or select an allocation for the reader.

02

Read the arithmetic mean separately from a growth forecast

The one-year portfolio return is 0.6 times A’s realized return plus 0.4 times B’s realized return. Taking its arithmetic mean gives 0.6 × 4% + 0.4 × 8% = 5.6%. Changing correlation leaves this mean unchanged when the weights and both asset means stay fixed.

An arithmetic mean describes a distribution’s average one-period return. It is not a promised return, a compound annual growth rate or a complete retirement projection. A multiyear calculation would need further assumptions about the sequence of returns, changing weights, contributions, withdrawals and costs. This calculator supplies none of those assumptions.

The capital input translates standard deviation into Canadian dollars. It does not change either asset’s return characteristics. Doubling the portfolio from CAD 100,000 to CAD 200,000 doubles the dollar translation while leaving the percentage mean and standard deviation unchanged.

03

Use the allocation curves to see the missing relationship

The first chart varies A’s weight from 0% to 100%, assigning the remainder to B. It compares the selected correlation with −0.5 and +1. At each endpoint only one asset remains, so all curves meet at that asset’s standalone standard deviation.

For nonnegative weights and correlation +1, portfolio standard deviation equals the weighted sum of the two standalone standard deviations. At the default weights, that sum is 0.6 × 6% + 0.4 × 18% = 10.8%. At correlation 0.2, the calculated standard deviation is about 8.67%. The difference comes from covariance, with the standalone risks held fixed.

Reducing correlation cannot increase variance in this particular two-asset, long-only comparison. It need not reduce risk below the risk of the safer individual asset at every weight. Nor does the result mean that adding any second holding improves every plan. The quantities and their relationship both matter.

04

A point on the scatter plot is an allocation

The horizontal coordinate of each point is calculated annual standard deviation. Its vertical coordinate is the assumed arithmetic mean return. Hollow points represent allocations at ten-percentage-point intervals; the larger filled point identifies the exact selected weight, including an intermediate weight if entered.

The default selected point is therefore approximately (8.67%, 5.60%). It is not an observed year, a simulated future outcome or an investor’s survey response. The chart plots alternative portfolios derived from the same inputs. The table identifies every allocation and both coordinates.

A point with a lower mean and at least as much standard deviation as another point has an unattractive comparison on those two selected measures. That observation does not establish a universally optimal investment. This small opportunity set omits taxes, liquidity, inflation exposure, downside asymmetry, restrictions and the household’s required payment dates.

05

Add variance terms before taking the square root

Write the weights as fractions wA and wB, standalone standard deviations as σA and σB, and correlation as ρ. Portfolio variance is wA²σA² + wB²σB² + 2wAwBρσAσB. Portfolio standard deviation is the square root of that total.

The waterfall uses squared percentage points to make the arithmetic readable. Its default first term is (0.6 × 6)² = 12.96. The second is (0.4 × 18)² = 51.84. The covariance cross term is 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 × 0.2 × 6 × 18 = 10.368. Together they produce variance of 75.168 squared percentage points. Its square root is approximately 8.66995 percentage points.

The chart labels round displayed values, while the calculation retains precision. These three variance components cannot be added as if they were three percentage returns. A negative covariance term reduces the variance total; it does not represent a payment, investment profit or negative standalone variance.

06

State a convention before calling something a risk contribution

The signed bars assign half of the weighted covariance cross term to A and half to B. On that stated convention, A receives 12.96 + 5.184 = 18.144 squared percentage points. B receives 51.84 + 5.184 = 57.024. Their sum reconciles to 75.168.

These figures describe contributions to variance. They are neither capital weights nor additive contributions to standard deviation. Reporting 18.144 as A’s percentage allocation would confuse the measurement unit and the question being answered.

A contribution can become negative. For example, keep the default weights and standalone risks but change correlation to −0.5. A’s attributed variance becomes 12.96 − 12.96 = 0; at correlation −1 it becomes −12.96. The other contribution offsets it so total variance stays nonnegative. This describes the model’s covariance relationship and does not establish a reliable real-world hedge.

07

Test the relationship instead of treating one estimate as permanent

The matrix varies both correlation and allocation. It holds the two standalone standard deviations fixed. At correlation −1, A’s 75% weight and B’s 25% weight give equal weighted standard deviations of 4.5 percentage points with perfectly opposite movements. Their modeled portfolio standard deviation is zero.

That cancellation requires an exact relationship in this idealized model. It is not evidence that an available pair of investments is risk-free. Estimated correlations depend on the observations, frequency, currency and measurement period; future relationships can differ. Zero correlation also does not generally establish statistical independence.

Standard deviation alone cannot specify the probability of losing money or the worst loss. Without a distributional assumption, “one standard deviation” is not a stated confidence interval. The default CAD 8,669.95 dollar translation is a dispersion measure for CAD 100,000, rather than a maximum loss, a reserve target or a guaranteed band around the mean.

08

Bring the chart back to the goal and payment calendar

Investor.gov’s asset-allocation overview connects allocation choices with investing horizon and risk tolerance. It also explains diversification across and within investment categories. Counting account names or fund wrappers does not by itself establish different underlying exposures.

For a real planning exercise, record the goal’s amount and date, identify money needed before a market recovery could be tolerated, and inspect the underlying investments. Then document how actual risk estimates were obtained and test plausible changes in the relationships. This article’s adjustable inputs illustrate those questions without answering them for a particular household.

The model has no leverage, short positions, taxes, fees, exchange-rate conversion, cash flows or trading constraints. Its calculations are a transparent starting point for understanding diversification. A complete plan must still fund the actual obligations and fit the investor’s capacity and willingness to bear losses.
